name: DNS Client (Resolver) Cache
os_min: Windows 2000 (DNS Client / Dnscache service); Get-DnsClientCache cmdlet requires Windows 8 / Server 2012+
location: In-memory cache maintained by the DNS Client (Dnscache) service; not persisted to disk. Related configuration lives at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Dnscache\Parameters (e.g. MaxCacheTtl). Viewed live via `ipconfig /displaydns` or PowerShell `Get-DnsClientCache`.
purpose: Speeds up repeat name resolution by caching successfully resolved DNS answers and negative (failed) lookups, and preloads static mappings from the local Hosts file; records which domain names a host recently attempted or succeeded in resolving.
key_fields: Record Type (A, AAAA, CNAME, PTR, SRV, etc.)
normal_baseline: Entries reflecting the browsing, telemetry, and update domains for applications actually running on the host, each with a TTL counting down from the value the authoritative DNS server supplied; Hosts file entries also appear here as preloaded records.
anomalies: Resolved entries for known C2/malicious domains or high-entropy, DGA-style hostnames
A legitimate domain resolving to an unexpected, attacker-controlled IP (upstream DNS hijack or cache poisoning)
Cache found empty during incident response with no corresponding reboot, suggesting ipconfig /flushdns or Clear-DnsClientCache was run to cover tracks
An unusually large number of distinct subdomains under one parent domain, consistent with DNS-based C2/tunneling
anti_forensic_notes: Entirely volatile, like the ARP cache: it lives only in the Dnscache service's memory and is wiped on reboot or by ipconfig /flushdns / Clear-DnsClientCache, so it must be collected during live response. A cache that is suspiciously empty on a system clearly used for recent browsing is itself a possible indicator that it was deliberately flushed.
